description: We are a team of six students from SMK Sacred Heart, Sibu, Sarawak, Malaysia. We are passionate about science, technology, AI, and space exploration. Through this challenge, we aim to analyze NASA’s flame experiment data and develop an interactive, AI-powered dashboard that transforms complex scientific findings into clear, meaningful insights. By combining teamwork, creativity, and data-driven thinking, we hope to contribute to a better understanding of flame behavior in microgravity and improve fire safety for future space missions.
summary: CubeSAT Mission: Save the Earth is an interactive, pixel-art space simulation game that allows players to design, build, launch and operate a CubeSat satellite to collect environmental data and address global challenges such as climate change, forest fires and ocean pollution. Players take on the roles of space mission team members and go through four main stages: mission selection, satellite assembly, orbital operations and mission debriefing. Throughout the game, they must select suitable equipment and manage limited resources, including mass, power, budget, data storage, communication and time, to ensure mission success. The project addresses the learning gap in aerospace education by making complex aerospace concepts easier to understand through interactive gameplay and teamwork. It also develops players' problem-solving and decision-making skills while demonstrating how satellite technology and scientific data can contribute to protecting Earth.
details:
CubeSat Mission: Save the Earth is a 2D pixel-art game in which players run a complete small-satellite mission from concept to operation. They choose a mission objective, collect materials, build a 3U CubeSat from trade-off-laden components, pick a launch option, fly the satellite through a live orbit simulation, analyse the science they bring home, and receive a graded mission report that explains why the mission succeeded or failed.

The game answers the challenge directly: every major design decision has a cost in mass, power, budget, data or time, and the consequences surface later in flight. Three Earth observation missions (storms, wildfires and ocean health) each stress a different resource, so there is no single perfect satellite. Players redesign and re-fly as often as they like.

It is built for learners with no space background. A guided tutorial teaches every system, and short in-game briefings explain each new mechanic when it first appears. The screen is organised into four crew stations (P1 Mission Planner, P2 Engineering, P3 Resources, P4 Controller), and a co-op mode lets two players share one mission in real time with distinct roles.

The game runs on Godot 4.7 for desktop and web (itch.io). It offers three missions plus a Freeplay sandbox and a Story campaign, three difficulty levels (Cadet, Engineer, Flight Director), and missions lasting 20, 25 or 30 simulated days, with fewer days on harder difficulties.

Players need to collect materials in the space station, craft CubeSat components and build an operable CubeSat to collect data from the Earth under fixed budget. The materials include energy cells, metal scraps and electronics parts. Every components require certain amount of materials and money. Players have to craft certain components to fulfil the requirement of mission while control the cost to prevent exceeding budget. Players should also consider the mass of each components as the maximum mass limit is 4 kg. To build an operable CubeSat, players need 1 sensor, 1-2 solar panels, 1-2 batteries, 1 antenna and 1 charger. Better components enable a better performance on CubeSat. Better solar panels can provide higher power supply. Better battery provide greater battery capacity. Better antenna provide higher data transmission rate. Better charger provide greater data storage and . When all five parts of components are equipped, without exceeding mass limit, a operable CubeSat is finally built and ready to be launched.
After the CubeSat is launched, players should start collecting data. This can be done by 5 keys, which are '1', '2', '3', 'a', 's', 'd' and 'w'. Pressing key '1' can turn on/off the sensor.

There are multiple difficulty level can be chosen by the players. The higher the difficulty level, the lower the budget given to buy the craft components to build the satellite. Therefore, players can do some task and small games to get extra budget.

In the ‘Freeplay’ mode,

In the story mode, there are three levels and interesting story line. Players can get an immersive experience in the game.

If they are bored along, they can also play with their friends. This game allow multiplayer!

Besides providing entertainment, our game also offers educational benefits by introducing players to satellite technology, space exploration and Earth's environmental challenges. Players can understand how CubeSats work and how satellite data can help monitor climate change, forest fires and ocean pollution. Our project combines education and gaming to create an interactive learning experience. Instead of simply reading scientific information, players can experience the process of planning a space mission, selecting satellite components, managing limited resources and completing different objectives. The creative aspect of our project is the combination of pixel-art graphics, mission-based gameplay, resource management and storytelling.

We designed different difficulty levels to make the game accessible to beginners while still providing challenges for experienced players. Throughout development, our team considered gameplay accessibility, educational value, resource limitations and user engagement. Our main goal is to make learning about space technology more interesting while encouraging players to understand the importance of using satellites to protect our planet.

How the game meets the challenge

The challenge asks for an interactive game in which participants design, manage and

simulate a complete space mission while making engineering decisions and managing

limited resources. Each part of that brief is a working system in CubeSat Mission.

A complete mission, concept to operation. Every mission runs the same four stages a

real team follows: choose the mission, build the satellite, launch and fly it, then

debrief.

Defining an objective and requirements first. Players open with a mission dossier

stating the science goal, the required instrument, the target orbit, a data goal (500,

750 or 1,000 MB), a time limit and a launch cost, before any building begins.

Designing a spacecraft and selecting instruments. A 3U CubeSat is built from five

subsystems (sensor, solar panels, battery, antenna and on-board computer and

storage), each with a simple and an advanced option that differ in mass, power, cost

and capability.

Choosing a launch vehicle and orbit. Players choose a rideshare or a dedicated

rocket, each mission flies a different orbit from 400 to 650 km, and an orbit-selection

task compares low Earth orbit with geostationary orbit.

Managing budget, mass, power, communications, data and lifetime. All six are live

resources on screen in flight and checked during design.

Seeing how decisions affect each other. A compare panel shows the mass, power

and cost change of every part swap, and flight problems such as brownouts, full

storage and weak links are traced back to the design in the report.

No single perfect solution. Each mission stresses a different resource, and the same

objective can be met by a cheap, light build flown carefully or a heavier, faster build

that leaves less money in reserve.

Simulation and evaluation. A real-time orbit models day and night, eclipses, ground

station passes, drag and solar flares, and ends in a graded report from S to F.

Feedback that explains why. A "What you learned" flight log names the cause of each

problem and how to fix it, and players can redesign and re-fly immediately.

Collaboration. Four labelled crew roles divide the work on screen, and a two-player

co-op mode shares one inventory, one budget and one satellite.

Accessible to every knowledge level. A guided tutorial, plain-English part

descriptions, visual indicators and three difficulty levels.

Game overview

Every mission follows the same four-stage loop that a real mission team follows, and the report sends players straight back into it with a better design.

1. Choose the mission (P1 Mission Planner). Read three mission dossiers, each with a

science goal, a required payload, an orbit, a data target, a duration and a launch cost.

An orbit preview shows where the targets are.

2. Build the satellite (P2 Engineering, P3 Resources). Walk a space station, collect raw

materials (metal scraps, electronic parts, energy cells), buy and craft components in

the Workshop, then assemble them on a 3U chassis in the Cleanroom. A launch

readiness checklist and a day/night stress test must pass before launch.

3. Launch and fly (P4 Controller). Operate the satellite in a real-time orbit simulation:

switch the sensor and transmitter on and off, point the spacecraft, manage the

battery through Earth's shadow, downlink to ground stations, and react to solar flares

and atmospheric drag.

4. Debrief. Play a short data-analysis game using the science collected, then read a

mission report with a grade from S to F, the numbers behind it and a plain-language

flight log of lessons. Replay with a new design or move on to the next mission.

The game has five modes:

Story Mode: a campaign of all three missions in order, framed by visual-novel scenes.

Grades carry money forward, and a D or F ends the run, so engineering quality

matters.

Multiplayer: two players share one mission with distinct roles (Pilot and Orbit

Keeper).

Freeplay: pick any mission and experiment freely; the sandbox for trying alternative

designs.

Tutorial: a guided first mission that teaches every system step by step.

Gallery: story artwork and gameplay screenshots to view at any time.

Between building and flying, the station also offers ten optional station tasks: short

engineering puzzles that earn extra mission funds (see Educational design).

Mission scenaent part of the design, so the satellite that wins one mission can fail another. Each has its own orbit, visuals, signature mechanic and data-analysis game.

Mission Alpha: Global Storm and Weather Watch. The goal is to track developing

hurricanes and cloud formations with an optical weather camera from a 400 km low Earth orbit. The low orbit gives fast, frequent passes, but atmospheric drag pulls the satellite down. The data target is 500 MB in 20 days, with a $16,000 launch. Storms drift and grow, and imaging a storm at peak strength yields up to 1.6x data. Afterwards, players rate storms by reading measured wind speed and assigning a Saffir-Simpson hurricane category.

Mission Beta: Wildfire and Thermal Anomaly Detector. The goal is to detect forest fires

and heat spikes early with an infrared thermal sensor from a 550 km sun-synchronous

orbit. Longer eclipse shadows demand strong batteries. The data target is 750 MB in 25 days, with a $20,000 launch. Fires spread over days, and data must be downlinked fast enough to warn firefighters in time. Afterwards, players find the wildfires by clicking every cell of a thermal image hot enough to be a fire.

Mission Gamma: Ocean and Reef Health Monitor. The goal is to measure ocean

temperature shifts, algae blooms and coastal pollution with a spectrometer and high

capacity storage from a 650 km orbit. The slower, higher orbit needs a stronger antenna to reach ground stations. The data target is 1,000 MB in 30 days, with a $24,000 launch.

Storage is limited and blooms need repeat visits to show how fast they spread.

Afterwards, players read a reflectance chart across blue, green, red and near-infrared

light to tell algae, oil and clear water apart.

The same objective can be met by different designs. A cheap optical build with frequent downlinks can finish Alpha; a heavier build with a high-gain dish and a compressing data unit moves data faster but leaves less money in reserve. The game rewards whichever balance delivers the data within budget and time.

Spacecraft design and payload

Players build a 3U CubeSat from five subsystem categories, choosing a simple or an

advanced part in each. No part is strictly better: every upgrade adds mass, power draw and cost.

Sensor (the science instrument). The optical camera costs $8,000, weighs 0.25 kg,

draws 3 W and collects 10 MB/s over targets, in daylight only. The IR / multispectral

sensor costs $22,000, weighs 0.6 kg, draws 8 W and collects 30 MB/s, day and night.

Solar panels (power generation). Body-mounted panels cost $5,000, weigh 0.2 kg and

give +5 W in sunlight; they cannot break. Deployable wings cost $15,000, weigh 0.5 kg

and give +15 W, unfolding in orbit.

Battery (power through Earth's shadow). The Li-ion cell battery costs $4,000, weighs

0.3 kg and holds 40 Wh. The high-density pack costs $11,000, weighs 0.7 kg and holds

100 Wh.

CubeSat Mission: Save the Earth — Project Description

Antenna (communications). The dipole costs $3,000, weighs 0.1 kg, draws 2 W and

uploads 15 MB/s at any angle, but weakens at high orbits. The high-gain dish costs

$14,000, weighs 0.45 kg, draws 5 W and uploads 45 MB/s, but must point at Earth.

Charger (on-board computer and data storage). The basic unit costs $5,000, weighs

0.15 kg and stores 150 MB. The compressing unit costs $16,000, weighs 0.3 kg, stores

400 MB and sends data 25% faster.

Building it. Parts cost money plus raw materials. Players walk the station's Science Lab, Storage Bay and SolarArea to collect electronic parts, metal scraps and energy cells, then craft parts in the Workshop. A clipboard checklist tracks one part per category and marks the mission's required payload ("REQ").

Assembling it. In the Cleanroom, parts are placed on a 3U chassis blueprint with six

mounts: antenna mount, top charger, solar mount, auxiliary mount, mid battery and sensor bottom. Parts can be detached and swapped at any time before launch.

Engineering simulation. The Cleanroom panel shows, live:

power generation against total drain with everything on, in watts a mass balance against the 4.0 kg limit of a 3U CubeSat a compare panel showing the mass, power and cost of the selected part against the one it replaces funds left after launch

a stress test that runs one simulated day/night cycle and reports whether the battery

survives the eclipse a launch-readiness checklist: power source, battery, antenna, charger and mission payload present; within mass limit; within budget

Proceed to Launch stays locked until every check is green, mirroring a real flight

readiness review.

Orbit and launch

Orbit and launch choices change what the satellite can do in flight, and the game checks that the spacecraft fits the chosen launch before it can fly.

Orbits with real characteristics. The three missions fly at 400, 550 and 650 km. Higher

orbits are slower, spend longer in Earth's shadow and sit further from ground stations, so they demand bigger batteries and stronger antennas. The 400 km orbit has frequent passes but suffers atmospheric drag, which the player counters with paid thruster boosts. The mission dossier explains each orbit in one plain sentence before the player commits.

Comparing orbit types. The Control Room station task "Find the correct orbit" asks

players to compare a 200 km orbit (drag brings it down in days), a 400 km low Earth orbit and a 35,786 km geostationary orbit (too far for a small camera to see storm detail). They choose the right one and watch a preview of the satellite circling at 400 km, 92 minutes per lap.

Launch vehicle choice. Each mission has a launch cost of $16,000 to $24,000. In the

Cleanroom, players choose a rideshare, which keeps the standard 4.0 kg 3U limit at no

extra cost, or a dedicated rocket, which raises the allowance to 5.0 kg for an extra $12,000.

Room for heavier, more capable parts is traded against budget.

Compatibility check. The readiness checklist compares the satellite's total mass with the

selected launch option's limit, and the total cost with the remaining budget. Launch is

blocked until both pass.

Orbit visualisation. Mission Select shows an orbit preview with target zones. In flight, the

orbit is drawn around Earth with the Sun's direction, the eclipse shadow ("umbra"),

drifting targets and ground-station cones.

Resource management

All six resources named in the brief are tracked, shown on screen at all times in flight, and

tied to each other through the design.

Mass is measured in kg against a 4.0 kg limit (5.0 kg with a dedicated rocket) on the

top bar and the Cleanroom balance. Every part adds mass, and advanced parts weigh

two to three times more; lighter parts or a paid dedicated rocket keep it in check.

Power shows as battery percentage and net watts (for example +3 W or -1 W), with

generation and drain bars. The sensor, antenna and computer draw power while

switched on, and eclipse gives 0 W. Bigger panels or batteries, switching systems off

in shadow, Sun-pointing and safe mode protect it.

Budget shows dollars left, starting at $78,000, $75,000 or $73,000 by difficulty. Parts,

the rocket, thruster boosts ($500 each) and daily operations spend it; a lean design,

station tasks and Story pay for good grades replenish it.

Data shows as on-board storage (for example 0/150 MB) and science goal (for

example 0/500 MB) bars. The sensor fills storage over targets; bigger or compressing

storage and frequent downlinks keep it flowing.

Communications shows signal strength and a "ground station lock" banner, with

station cones over Europe, Asia and North America. Downlink only works inside a

cone, at the antenna's rate; a high-gain dish pointed at Earth and a compressing data

unit speed it up.

Time shows as a day counter against the mission limit (for example Day 0/18). Every

orbit uses time, and 1x, 2x and 4x time warp speed up quiet stretches; efficient

operations reach the data goal sooner.

How they interact. A faster sensor fills storage sooner, so it needs more storage or more downlink time. The dish that empties storage faster must point at Earth, which takes the panels off the Sun. The extra battery that survives a long eclipse adds mass, which can force a dedicated rocket and cost budget. Players feel these links during flight rather than reading them in a rulebook.

Which resource is critical depends on the mission. Alpha is limited by drag and time,

Beta by power and downlink (long eclipses and urgent fire warnings), and Gamma by

storage and communications (more data, a slower orbit and higher altitude).

Mission simulation and operations

After launch the player becomes mission control: the design is fixed, and every weakness in it shows up as a real-time operating problem.

The mission dashboard. A top bar shows mass, power, budget, data, comms and time; the bottom console holds the controls; the right panel shows the science goal, on-board storage, day count and orbit number.

Controls and their trade-offs.

Payload sensor (key 1) collects science data over targets, but draws power, is wasted

off-target and fills storage.

Transmit (key 2) downlinks stored data inside a ground-station cone, but draws

power and only works over a station.

Safe mode (key 3) hibernates systems to protect electronics, but stops science and

downlink while on.

Attitude, Sun or Nadir (W, A, S, D) points the panels at the Sun or the instrument and

dish at Earth, trading power against observing and communicating.

CubeSat Mission: Save the Earth — Project Description

Time warp (1x, 2x, 4x; Q and E) speeds up quiet stretches, leaving less time to react

to events.

Thruster boost (T) raises the orbit against drag for $500 each.

What the simulation models.

Day and night: solar panels give 0 W in Earth's shadow, and the battery must carry the

load.

Brownouts: a flat battery reboots the satellite and loses stored data.

Ground-station passes: downlink only inside a station's cone, at the antenna's rate.

Storage limits: data collected with full storage is lost.

Atmospheric drag at low altitude: the orbit decays unless boosted.

Random events: solar flares give a short warning, then corrupt stored data unless the

player switches to safe mode. They are rare on Cadet and frequent on Flight Director.

Mission-specific targets: drifting, growing storms (Alpha); spreading fires that need

timely alerts (Beta); blooms that need repeat visits (Gamma).

Guidance in flight. Callouts such as "Over target - sensor on (1)" and "Ground station lock:

Europe" teach the timing of operations, and a short briefing pauses the first mission of each type to explain its new mechanic.

Evaluation, scoring and post-mission analysis

Every mission ends in a Mission Summary Report that scores the result, shows the

numbers behind it and explains in plain words what caused success or failure and how to fix it.

What the report shows. Data collected and transmitted against the goal; power

efficiency (Wh in against Wh out, and the number of brownouts); total budget spent

against the budget, with a bonus for money left unspent; mission duration against the

limit; a mission success rate; a final orbit replay; and a grade stamp.

How the score is built. The success rate weighs data delivered (50%), budget efficiency

(25%) and operations (25%), with power health included. Mission-specific penalties

apply, such as late or missed wildfire warnings in Beta. The data-analysis game afterwards adds up to 4 points per correct answer, so understanding the science can lift a grade.

Grades. S, A and B all require the mission goal to be met: S needs a score of 90 or more, A needs 75 or more, and B is any successful mission. C (50 or more) and D (30 or more) are for missions that missed the goal but were not aborted. F is anything lower, or an aborted mission, for example when the orbit decays or the money runs out. In Story Mode the grade sets the next mission's budget, from $90,000 for S down to $50,000 for D, so good engineering compounds; a D or F ends the campaign.

"What you learned" flight log. The report explains causes, not just outcomes.

Examples of lines the game writes from what actually happened:

"Your battery ran flat 2 times in Earth's shadow. A bigger battery, or switching the

sensor off in eclipse, avoids reboots and lost data."

"On-board storage was full for 40% of your target passes. A bigger charger or more

frequent downlinks captures more science."

"The dipole loses signal strength at higher orbits. A high-gain dish keeps the link

strong from 650 km."

"Atmospheric drag pulled the satellite down. Low orbits need regular thruster boosts

(T) to stay up."

"A solar flare corrupted stored data. Safe mode (3) during the warning shields the

electronics."

"You finished with $12,000 unspent. A lean design leaves room for a bigger science

payload next time."

Mission-specific lines: data captured at peak storm strength; fires spotted and

warnings delivered in time or late; how many times blooms were measured.

Redesign and re-fly. The report offers Replay with New Design, Try Next Mission or Main

Menu, so players can iterate on the same objective until they find a balance that works.

Collaboration and team play

The mission is split into team responsibilities, and in co-op the result depends on how well

both players coordinate.

Four crew stations. Each stage of the game belongs to a labelled role, shown as a badge

on screen, so a team of up to four gathered around one game can divide the work the way

a real mission team does:

P1 Mission Planner chooses the mission, reads the requirements and owns the

required payload (Mission Select and the Cleanroom payload banner).

P2 Engineering handles spacecraft configuration, and attitude and pointing in flight

(the Cleanroom and attitude control).

CubeSat Mission: Save the Earth — Project Description

P3 Resources watches budget, mass, power and the rocket choice (the Cleanroom

resources panel).

P4 Controller runs flight operations: sensor, transmit, safe mode, time warp and

boosts (the orbit console).

Two-player co-op. One player creates a room and shares a short room code; the other

joins. In the lobby they agree on difficulty, mission or Story Mode and roles, and the game starts when both press Ready.

Pilot: builds and flies the satellite.

Orbit Keeper: walks the same station, collects materials, crafts and attaches parts

alongside the Pilot, then keeps the satellite in orbit during flight by typing. Air drag

pulls the satellite down, and every correct letter pushes it back up. The target speed

is 60, 80 or 100 words per minute by difficulty.

Shared everything: one material inventory, one budget and one satellite. Both players

can attach parts at the same time, and each sees the other walking the station and on the minimap.

Negotiation built in. Because money, materials and the 4 kg mass limit are shared, players must agree which parts to buy and which to give up. If the Keeper cannot hold the typing speed, the orbit decays and the report says so, so the final grade reflects the team, not one player.

Educational design

The game teaches by letting players make a decision, see its consequence and learn why, instead of marking answers right or wrong. Concepts are introduced inside play, in plain English.

The tutorial. A guided five-day first mission covers, step by step:

1. The station, the parts clipboard and the HUD.

2. Why a satellite needs each of the five categories: the sensor is its eyes, the charger

its brain and memory, the antenna its link to Earth, the battery its power through

Earth's shadow, and solar panels its electricity, with more power costing more mass.

3. Collecting materials and crafting parts, including what costs mean and what "REQ"

parts are.

4. Assembling the satellite and passing the readiness checklist.

5. Flight: sunlight and shadow, targets, ground stations, storage against the science

goal, switching the sensor and transmitter, and responding to low power.

6. A practice round of all three data-analysis games.

Briefings on new mechanics. The first time a player meets drifting storms, spreading

fires, limited storage and revisits, or an analysis game, a short step-by-step briefing

explains what to do and why.

Data-analysis games use real science methods.

Saffir-Simpson scale: rating hurricanes from measured wind speed.

Thermal imaging: finding fire pixels by temperature.

Spectral signatures: telling algae, oil and clear water apart by how they reflect blue,

green, red and near-infrared light.

Ten station tasks: engineering puzzles in the rooms. These optional jobs are listed on a second clipboard page, each naming its room and apparatus and paying mission funds.

Mission Alpha: The Broken Circuit at the Lab computer, rotating tiles to route power

from a source to a load ($1,400); Find the Missing Toolkit for the Storage engineer,

searching the station and returning equipment ($1,400); Catch the Sunlight at the

solar panel controls, where panel angle to the Sun sets power output ($1,400); and

Find the Correct Orbit at the orbit planner, comparing 200 km, 400 km LEO and

35,786 km GEO ($1,800).

Mission Beta: The Heat Signature Mystery at the thermal scanner, picking regions

above a temperature threshold, with a note that 60°C is a game rule, not a real-world

threshold ($1,600); The Overweight Shipment at the digital scale, keeping every

required item within a mass limit ($2,000); and Match the Satellite Signals at the

comms computer, recognising sine, square, sawtooth and triangle waves ($2,400).

Mission Gamma: Decode the Ocean Data at the research computer, comparing red,

green and blue channels to find algae blooms ($2,000); Balance the Cargo on the

cargo platform, balancing loads within a tolerance and a weight limit ($2,000); and The

Energy Network at the power panel, distributing limited power where longer cables

lose more ($2,000).

Visual indicators everywhere. Coloured bars, red and green checklist items, warnings

such as "High power draw!", part cards with three short pros and cons, and a mass balance that tips as parts are added.

Difficulty, replayability, story and presentation

Three difficulty levels tighten the same real constraints rather than adding artificial ones,

so the lessons stay true at every level.

Cadet: a $78,000 budget, rare solar flares (about every 10 days), the full mission time

and a 60 WPM co-op typing target.

Engineer: a $75,000 budget, more frequent flares (about every 7 days), 2 days less

mission time and an 80 WPM typing target.

Flight Director: a $73,000 budget, frequent flares (about every 4 days), 3 days less

mission time and a 100 WPM typing target.

Replayability. Three missions across three difficulties, a simple or advanced part in each

of five categories, two launch options, randomised storm, fire and bloom positions,

random solar flares and randomised station-task puzzles mean no two runs play the same.

Freeplay lets players test alternative designs without campaign pressure.

Story Mode. A short visual-novel campaign frames why the missions matter: Earth's

problems, the student team, a lecture on the mission, and title cards before each mission.

Between missions the story reacts to what was found: a forest-fire crisis leads into Beta, a

strange green patch in the ocean leads into Gamma, and an ending shows the improved

Earth. Grades carry funds from one mission to the next.

Presentation. Consistent pixel art at 640 x 360, a walkable space station with labelled

rooms, a pixel Earth with day and night sides, separate music for menus, the station and flight, and sound effects for walking, collecting, buying and each grade band. A volume control sits in every pause menu.

Technical implementation

The game is a self-contained Godot 4.7 project written in GDScript, playable in a web

browser on itch.io and as a desktop download.

Rendering. Every screen, part, room and chart is drawn in code at a fixed 640 x 360

resolution with integer scaling and a custom 5 x 7 pixel font, keeping the pixel look

crisp at any window size.

Structure. Twelve screens (title, mission select, station, cleanroom, orbit, report,

story, gallery, multiplayer lobby, typing station, analysis and station tasks) share one

global game-state module holding missions, parts, inventory, budget and results.

CubeSat Mission: Save the Earth — Project Description

Data-driven design. Missions, parts, difficulty levels and station tasks are tables of

numbers (cost, mass, watts, data rate, storage, orbit, targets), so balancing or adding

content means editing data, not code.

Simulation. A fixed-step model of orbit position, sunlight and eclipse, battery charge

and drain, storage, downlink rate in ground-station cones, drag and altitude, and timed

random events.

Multiplayer. The Pilot's game is the single source of truth. The Orbit Keeper's actions

are applied instantly on their own screen and sent to the Pilot, who sends back the

shared state. Players connect through a small relay server using room codes over

WebSockets, which works in browsers and across different networks.

Controls. Keyboard and mouse throughout, with on-screen key hints on every

console.

Optional features from the brief

The brief lists features that teams may consider. CubeSat Mission includes these:

Multiple mission scenarios with different objectives: storms, wildfires and ocean

health, each with its own orbit, payload, mechanic and analysis game.

Random events and unexpected constraints: solar flares, brownouts, drifting storms,

spreading fires and orbit decay.

Different difficulty levels: Cadet, Engineer and Flight Director.

A simplified spacecraft model with realistic trade-offs: a 3U CubeSat with a 4 kg

class mass limit and five subsystems.

Interactive spacecraft visualisation: a click-to-place chassis blueprint, and the

satellite drawn in orbit and in the final orbit replay.

A mission dashboard with real-time resource consumption: mass, power, budget,

data, comms, time and storage on the flight HUD.

Mission reports at the end of each simulation: the Mission Summary Report with its

grade and numbers.

Post-mission analysis explaining success or failure: the "What you learned" flight log

with causes and fixes.

Cooperative missions for teams: four on-screen crew roles and two-player Pilot and

Orbit Keeper co-op.

A sandbox mode: Freeplay, with any mission and free experimentation inside real

constraints.

In short: CubeSat Mission lets a beginner define a mission, design and launch a spacecraft

under real constraints, operate it, and learn from a report that explains every outcome, alone or with a teammate.
